# Deciding whether a line is the right model {#sec-linear-models-reflection}















Imagine the review arrives, and in the margin of the second page, between a comment about the antibody dilution and a request for a larger font, someone has written: "Why a linear model?" You open the lab notebook looking for an answer (@fig-reflection-margin). What you find, if you are honest, is the answer most of us would give at eleven at night: because it is what I know how to do, because the tutorial did it, because the last paper in this journal did it. That is an explanation of your habits. It is not a reason about your data, and the reviewer (who, by the way, is probably asking because their own last model failed in an interesting way) knows the difference.

![A pencilled question in the margin of the review: "why a line?" Your habits are an explanation of you. Your data deserve a reason.](images/linear-models-reflection_margin-note-in-manuscript.png){#fig-reflection-margin fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of an open printed manuscript on a wooden desk, with wavy lines for text, a small figure of a line through dots with error bars, and a red pencil circle around a block of text with a curved arrow leading to a hand-drawn question mark. A red pencil lies across the page and a cup of tea sits in the corner."}

This chapter exists to give you a better answer. We are not going to learn a new technique here. We have spent four chapters building one line, and what I want to do now is walk back through them and read what we actually did, because every chapter contained a decision, and each decision had a price. Then I want to put the line next to its neighbors, answering the same question about the same animals, so that you can see what you buy and what you pay with each choice. If you finish the chapter wanting to say "a line, because..." and then finish the sentence with something about your question, your outcome and your design, it has done its job.

## A line is a bundle of decisions

In @sec-linear-regression-assumptions we met McElreath's golem, the clay robot that does exactly what you tell it and has no opinion on whether you told it the right thing [@mcelreath2020]. The equation $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i$ is that golem. Fitting it with `lm()` or `brm()` is not a neutral act, like weighing a sample. It is a bet that your data behave in a few specific ways, and the software will place the bet for you without a murmur whether or not it is a good one.

Spelled out (@fig-reflection-bets), the bet has five parts. You bet that the outcome is a continuous quantity that can sit anywhere on the number line, so that a bell curve around the mean is a fair account of the scatter. You bet that effects add up: that a day costs the same amount of tissue wherever you are along the time axis, and that two predictors can be summed. You bet that the scatter is about the same size for every animal, so one $\sigma$ suffices. You bet that each row brings its own information, that no two rows are echoes of each other. And you bet that the question you are asking is one a line can answer, which is usually a question about *how much* something changes on average, not about, say, which of two mechanisms is at work.

![Fitting a line is five bets placed at once: bell-shaped scatter, effects that add up, one spread, independent rows, and a question a line can answer.](images/linear-models-reflection_five-bets-on-a-table.png){#fig-reflection-bets fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a green gaming table with five round chips in an arc, each marked with a simple icon: a bell curve on a teal chip, a straight arrow on an ochre chip, a double-headed arrow on a pink chip, a chain link on a green chip and a question mark on a grey-blue chip, with a die beside them."}

None of those bets is exotic, and in many datasets all five hold well enough that a line is an excellent choice. That is the first half of the message of this chapter, and I would hate for you to read the rest as a sermon against linear models. The second half is that none of them is guaranteed either, and that nothing in statistics makes the line the default you must justify leaving. "Linear regression is where you start" is advice about workflow, something that depends on the field and on the person giving it. It is not a rule that says other models need to apply for permission. The books this one leans on say the same thing in their own voices. McElreath calls linear regression the geocentric model of applied statistics: a descriptive model that fits many different stories about how the data arose, useful as long as you do not read its structure too literally [@mcelreath2020]. Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari describe the working cycle as starting with simple linear models and expanding them with predictors, interactions and transformations when your checks and your goal ask for it [@gelman2020], and the *Bayesian Workflow* authors put it as starting with simple models you understand and complicating them as needed [@gelman2026]. And the famous line that all models are wrong but some are useful [@box1976] is read by Inchausti as a statement that models are provisional scaffolds [@inchausti2023], whose practical consequence McElreath spells out: the goal is not to ask whether the assumptions are true, since they are not, but to assess exactly how the model fails to describe the data [@mcelreath2020].

The useful question, then, is never "can I use `lm()`?" Of course you can; it will run. The useful question is the one we asked of the equation in @sec-linear-regression-what: what is the value of knowing the predictor, given what *my* question, *my* outcome and *my* design need from the model? The rest of the chapter is a way of answering it with data we already know.

## What happened to each bet in `cell_data`

I find it easiest to keep score. @tbl-reflection_conditions takes the five bets and says what became of each one in the tissue-area story and its neighbors. It is not a second copy of @tbl-assumptions_map, which lists the conditions and what each protects; that table is the theory, and this one is the verdict on one dataset, with the chapter where you can see the evidence.

| Bet | What happened in `cell_data` | Where |
|:-----------------|:--------------------------------------|:--------------|
| The outcome is continuous and unbounded | Tissue area, yes. PDGFR-β+ cell counts from the same animals, no: a Gaussian model gives a 25% chance of a negative count for a sham animal | @sec-count-regression |
| Effects add up (one slope over the whole range) | Over 0 to 30 days, no: the straight line misses a day's mean by up to 2.3 mm². Over 3 to 14 days, yes: about 0.74 mm² lost per day early on and 0.64 later | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous |
| One spread fits every animal | No: the day-3 standard deviation is 3.1 mm², against 1.1 and 1.0 at days 7 and 14 | @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous, @sec-linear-regression-multiple |
| Each row is an independent observation | Yes, by design: 49 rows, 49 animals. It stops being true the moment you go below the animal | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions |
| The question is one a line can answer | A rate of tissue loss in a window, yes. A different trajectory for sham and ischemic animals, not with these data | @sec-linear-regression-multiple |

: What became of each bet a linear model makes, on the dataset of this part. {#tbl-reflection_conditions}

Let me retell the rows as the story they are, because the order in which they happened matters.

**The line across everything failed, and we could see how.** In @sec-linear-regression-what we drew one straight line from day 0 to day 30, and I told you it looked wrong. In @sec-linear-regression-assumptions we found out why: the mean residuals by day (-0.89, 2.27, 0.42, -2.13, 0.82 mm² at days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30) were not noise around a line but a shape, a bump at day 3 followed by a decline that flattens. One more thing hides in that comparison. The animals at "day 0" are the 7 shams, and no sham exists at any later day, so the step from day 0 to day 3 mixes time with being operated on.

**The window rescued the line, and it cost us something.** We kept days 3, 7 and 14, where the loss per day is nearly constant, and estimated a slope of -0.67 [-0.82, -0.53] mm² per day. That is a useful, honest number. It is also the product of a choice I made after looking at the means, and a different analyst could have drawn the window elsewhere. The name for this is [researcher degrees of freedom]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: picture a garden path that forks every few steps, so that the walk you ended up taking was one of many you could have taken, and the one you report was shaped by what you saw along the way. I do not think the window is wrong. I think its price is that the slope is a statement about days 3 to 14 and nothing more, and that I should not pretend I would have chosen it blind. Harrell's advice to pre-specify models as much as possible [@harrell2015] is advice for the experiments you have not run yet; for this one, the honest move was to say so, and we did.

**One $\sigma$ was wrong for one day.** Even inside the window, the spread at day 3 (3.1 mm²) is about three times that of days 7 and 14, and one $\sigma$ averages over them. The slope survived this; a prediction interval for a new day-3 animal would not.

**GFAP vanished once we knew the day.** Alone, GFAP had a slope of -0.40 [-0.84, 0.04] per 100 units of integrated density; with `DPI` in the model it was 0.05 [-0.21, 0.31]. It was never a rival explanation, only a passenger on time. A log2 transformation of GFAP then bought us nothing: the residual $\sigma$ went from 1.82 to 1.84.

**`Condition * DPI` was not a statistical failure at all.** Shams exist only at day 0 and ischemic animals only from day 3 onward, so no model, linear or otherwise, can tell you whether the trajectories differ. That is a decision for the experiment, made before a single section was cut, and it is the clearest example in the book of a question the design had already closed.

**And a different outcome from the same animals changed the whole family.** The PDGFR-β+ counts live in `cell_data` too. The Gaussian line we have trusted for four chapters expects a negative count for 25% of new sham animals, and a spread that does not grow with the mean, when the counts really fan out from a standard deviation of about 190 cells at day 0 to about 925 at day 7. Nothing about the dataset changed. The outcome did, and with it the model that makes sense. [The introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) is the answer, and it opens the next part of the book.

::: callout-tip
Read the list again and notice who found out each failure. In no case was it a test. A picture showed the shape, a table showed the spread, and the design told us about the interaction before the first model was fitted. That is the habit @sec-appendix-assumption-tests argues for with simulated data, and here it is on real ones.
:::

## The same question, five answers

Suppose the reviewer is satisfied with your reasons and now asks something harder: "Fine, but would another model have told you something different?" It is a good question, and the way to answer it is to ask several models the *same* thing. Our question will be the one a lab-meeting audience would care about: **how much tissue area changes between day 7 and day 14.**

I have five answers to that question. Four come from models you have already met, read from the caches of the earlier chapters (nothing is refitted here), and the fifth needs no model at all.

1. The straight line across the whole range, 0 to 30 days (@sec-linear-regression-assumptions).
2. The straight line in the window, 3 to 14 days (@sec-linear-regression-single-continuous).
3. One mean per day within the window, with one common $\sigma$ (@sec-linear-regression-multiple).
4. One mean *and one spread* per day over the whole range, from the appendix (@sec-appendix-assumption-tests).
5. No model: the difference between the observed means of day 7 and day 14.

A word on why the fourth model, fitted on days 0 to 30, can sit beside the others. Its estimate of the day-7 to day-14 change is made from the same 11 animals at day 7 and 12 at day 14 that the window uses, because each day has its own mean and its own spread. The other days cannot influence this contrast. So the models are not answering different questions with different animals; they differ in what they assume.

Before the numbers, a picture of the data with what each model draws (@fig-reflection_four_answers), because the comparison is easier to feel than to read. I use a plain scatter with every animal visible (there are only 49, and I would not hide any of them behind a summary), the observed mean of each day as a black diamond, and the two straight lines labeled directly on the plot, so you do not have to go back and forth to a legend. Color and line type carry the same distinction twice, so it survives a grayscale printout.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The observed mean of each day, for the black diamonds
means_df <- data.frame(DPI = as.numeric(names(mean_day)), area = as.numeric(mean_day))

# Intercept and slope of the two straight lines, from the cached fits
b_full <- fixef(fit_line_full)[, "Estimate"]
b_win <- fixef(fit_line_win)[, "Estimate"]

# End points of each line over the range it covers
seg_full <- data.frame(DPI = c(0, 30))
seg_full$area <- b_full["Intercept"] + b_full["DPI"] * seg_full$DPI
seg_win <- data.frame(DPI = c(3, 14))
seg_win$area <- b_win["Intercept"] + b_win["DPI_c"] * (seg_win$DPI - 3)

# Every animal, the two lines (labelled directly on the plot) and the day means
ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.4, height = 0, color = "grey45", alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = seg_full, aes(y = area), color = "#D55E00", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = seg_win, aes(y = area), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(data = means_df, aes(y = area), shape = 18, size = 5, color = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = 16.5, y = 12.6, label = "Line, days 0 to 30", color = "#D55E00",
           hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = 8.2, label = "Line, days 3 to 14", color = "#0072B2",
           hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Tissue area by day after ischemia, with the observed mean of each day (black diamonds) and the two straight lines fitted in earlier chapters. The dashed line crosses the whole range, the solid one only the window from day 3 to day 14.](linear-models-reflection_files/figure-html/fig-reflection_four_answers-1.png){#fig-reflection_four_answers fig-alt='Scatter of tissue area in mm² at 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days with a black diamond at each day\'s mean. A dashed orange line declines gently across the whole range and passes well below the diamonds at day 3 and above them at day 14. A solid blue line from day 3 to day 14 passes through the diamonds at days 3, 7 and 14.' width=624}
:::
:::






The dashed line is the one that does not touch the diamonds where the interesting things happen, and the solid one is the one that does. Notice also what the figure cannot say. It says nothing about the spread, which is the other half of what the models disagree about. For that we need the posterior of the quantity we agreed to ask about, so let me compute it from each model's draws and plot the answers on one axis (@fig-reflection_change_7_14). A half-eye is the honest glyph here: some of these intervals are lopsided or narrow in ways a bare interval would flatten, and the *width* of each answer is half of what I want you to see.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The four models whose answer we plot, in display order
model_levels <- c("Line, days 0 to 30",
                  "Line, days 3 to 14",
                  "One mean per day, days 3 to 14",
                  "Mean and spread per day, days 0 to 30")

# One row per posterior draw per model: the change between day 7 and day 14
change_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = model_levels[1], change = change_full),
  data.frame(model = model_levels[2], change = change_win_line),
  data.frame(model = model_levels[3], change = change_win_day),
  data.frame(model = model_levels[4], change = change_free)
)
change_df$model <- factor(change_df$model, levels = rev(model_levels))

# Half-eye per model; the dashed line is the difference of the observed means
ggplot(change_df, aes(x = change, y = model, fill = model)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = change_obs, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Line, days 0 to 30" = "#D55E00",
                               "Line, days 3 to 14" = "#0072B2",
                               "One mean per day, days 3 to 14" = "#56B4E9",
                               "Mean and spread per day, days 0 to 30" = "#009E73")) +
  labs(x = "Change in tissue area from day 7 to day 14 (mm²)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Change in tissue area between day 7 and day 14 under four models. Dots mark medians, thick and thin bars the 50% and 95% credible intervals; the dashed line is the difference of the observed means.](linear-models-reflection_files/figure-html/fig-reflection_change_7_14-1.png){#fig-reflection_change_7_14 fig-alt='Four half-eye plots. The straight line over the whole range is centered near minus 1.9 mm² with a narrow interval. The window line, the one-mean-per-day model and the mean-and-spread-per-day model are centered between minus 4.4 and minus 4.8 mm², with intervals that overlap each other and the dashed line at minus 4.5, and none overlap the whole-range line.' width=768}
:::
:::






Read it from top to bottom. The line across the whole range says the loss is about -1.9 [-2.4, -1.5] mm², with a narrow interval. Every other model puts it between -4.7 and -4.5 mm², and the observed means differ by -4.49. The whole-range line is not just slightly off. Its interval does not overlap with any of the others. This is the failure we saw by eye, now expressed in the units of the question, and it is why I keep saying the line is not wrong because it is a line. It is wrong because I asked one slope to describe a rise, a fall and a plateau. Give the same kind of model a stretch where the decline is nearly steady, and it agrees with models that make no assumption about shape at all.

The agreement among the three good answers is real but not perfect, and the differences are informative. The window line gives -4.7 [-5.7, -3.7], narrower than the one-mean-per-day model's -4.5 [-6.2, -2.9]. A line spends one parameter on the whole decline, and that is why it is sharper: it pools information across the three days under a promise of straightness. And the one-mean-per-day model is wider than the model that also frees the spread, -4.5 [-5.5, -3.6], because its single $\sigma$ is dragged up by the noisy day 3 and applied to the calm days 7 and 14. The free-spread model estimates a $\sigma$ of about 1.1 and 1.1 mm² for those two days, against 3.2 at day 3, and its interval for this contrast is the one that is closest to what the animals at days 7 and 14 actually scatter like.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

The agreement is not an artifact of the Bayesian fits. With no prior doing real work, as in every model of this part, the frequentist versions land in the same places: the straight line in the window and the model with free spreads, fitted with `lm()` and with `glmmTMB` (whose `dispformula` models the spread, something `parsnip` has no engine for), both appear below.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(glmmTMB)

# Straight line in the window by least squares; the change over 7 days and its 95% interval
lm_win <- lm(Tissue_Area ~ I(DPI - 3), data = win)
est_win <- 7 * coef(lm_win)[2]
ci_win <- 7 * confint(lm_win)[2, ]

# One mean and one spread per day (dispformula models the spread), by maximum likelihood
free_tmb <- glmmTMB(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, dispformula = ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)
# Day-14 minus day-7 mean and its standard error (variance of a difference)
b <- fixef(free_tmb)$cond
V <- vcov(free_tmb)$cond
est_free <- unname(b["DPI_f14"] - b["DPI_f7"])
se_free <- sqrt(V["DPI_f14", "DPI_f14"] + V["DPI_f7", "DPI_f7"] - 2 * V["DPI_f14", "DPI_f7"])
```
:::






The window line gives -4.7 mm² (95% confidence interval -5.7 to -3.7) and the free-spread model gives -4.5 (-5.3 to -3.7), against -4.7 [-5.7, -3.7] and -4.5 [-5.5, -3.6] from `brms`. The two lenses agree because, with 31 or 49 animals and diffuse priors, the likelihood does nearly all the work. What differs from model to model is the assumption, not the lens.
:::













All 6 fits used in this chapter pass the sampler checks of @sec-mcmc-model-checking (worst Rhat 1.004, smallest effective sample size 1318, 0 divergent transitions in total). That vouches for the sampling and says nothing about whether any of these models describes the biology, which is the question the rest of the chapter is about.

Now the ledger. @tbl-reflection_models sets the five answers side by side with what each assumes and what it costs, because the number in the previous figure is only half of an honest comparison. The other half is the price tag.

| Answer | Question it answers | What it assumes | What it costs |
|:------------------|:---------------------|:------------------|:------------------------------|
| Line, days 0 to 30 | How fast does area change, if one rate described the whole month? | A constant rate, one $\sigma$, Gaussian errors | Wrong on average at two of five days; the change from day 7 to 14 comes out at -1.9 [-2.4, -1.5] mm², with a narrow interval |
| Line, days 3 to 14 | How fast does area fall inside the window? | The decline is straight between day 3 and day 14; one $\sigma$ | The window was chosen after looking at the means; silent about days 0 and 30; too small a $\sigma$ at day 3 |
| One mean per day, days 3 to 14 | What is the mean on each day I measured? | Nothing about shape between the days; one $\sigma$ | One parameter per day; nothing to say about a day I did not sample; the day-3 spread inflates every interval |
| Mean and spread per day, days 0 to 30 | What are the mean and the scatter on each measured day? | Nothing about shape or spread; independent animals | Two parameters per day, the spread of a day estimated from as few as 7 animals; nothing between measured days |
| No model | What did these animals do? | Nothing | No interval and no statement about new animals |

: Five answers to the same question, what each one assumes and what it costs. {#tbl-reflection_models}

Notice that no row is "the right model". Each row is a different trade between what it takes for granted and what it lets you say. Choosing among them is a decision about your question and about your audience, not a procedure to be run.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** Tissue area fell by 4.7 [3.7, 5.7] mm² between day 7 and day 14 under a straight line fitted to days 3 to 14 (posterior median and 95% credible interval), by 4.5 [2.9, 6.2] mm² with one mean per day, and by 4.5 [3.6, 5.5] mm² with a separate mean and spread per day; the observed means differed by 4.49 mm². A straight line fitted to the whole 0 to 30 day course gave 1.9 [1.5, 2.4] mm², which we did not interpret because it failed the model checks.

**Methods.** We chose the window from day 3 to day 14 after inspecting the day means, and we report conclusions only for that window. We assessed the line with residual plots by day and posterior predictive checks of the mean and standard deviation of each day, and we repeated the analysis with models that make fewer assumptions about shape and spread.
:::

## Do you need a model at all?

The last row of the table looks like a joke, and it is not. Suppose the question at the lab meeting is simply "what happened to these 31 animals between day 3 and day 14?" Then the answer is on the page (@fig-reflection_descriptive).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Per day: number of animals, mean and SD of tissue area
desc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(win, win$DPI), function(g) {
  data.frame(DPI = factor(g$DPI[1]), n = nrow(g), mean = mean(g$Tissue_Area), sd = sd(g$Tissue_Area))
}))

# Every animal as a point, with each day's mean and SD beside it in orange
ggplot(win, aes(x = factor(DPI), y = Tissue_Area)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, color = "grey35", alpha = 0.75, size = 2.2) +
  geom_pointrange(data = desc, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                  color = "#D55E00", shape = 18, size = 1, linewidth = 1,
                  position = position_nudge(x = 0.28)) +
  geom_text(data = desc, aes(y = 4.6, label = paste0("n = ", n)), size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(4, 21)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Tissue area of every animal in the window, with the mean and plus or minus one standard deviation of each day (orange). No model is involved.](linear-models-reflection_files/figure-html/fig-reflection_descriptive-1.png){#fig-reflection_descriptive fig-alt='Strip plot of tissue area at days 3, 7 and 14 with an orange diamond and bar at each day\'s mean and standard deviation. The spread at day 3 is visibly wider than at days 7 and 14. Sample sizes of 8, 11 and 12 are printed under each column.' width=624}
:::
:::






Every animal is visible, and so is the fact that day 3 is the scattered one. You can say, without any model, that the mean fell from 16.9 to 13.9 to 9.5 mm², and that the day-3 animals disagreed with each other much more than the later ones. For a figure legend in a thesis chapter, that is a complete and honest description.

Notice how that figure was built, because it follows the habits the books we lean on recommend for describing data honestly. Every animal is drawn, instead of a bar with a whisker that hides the sample size and any lopsided distribution, and the spread is a standard deviation, which describes how the animals scatter, not a standard error, which describes how precisely a mean is estimated under a model and shrinks as the sample grows. The sample size is printed on the plot, and the interpretation stays on the side of "this is what these animals did". That last habit matters: a descriptive analysis is a different kind of claim from a confirmatory one, and the two should not be blended in the same paragraph.

What the picture cannot give you is an interval, or a statement about the next animal. The difference of the observed means between day 7 and day 14, -4.49 mm², is a fact about these 23 animals. Gelman and colleagues give three reasons to fit a regression when you could simply plot the raw data: it condenses a pattern into a summary you can carry around, it quantifies the uncertainty that a scatterplot or a sample mean cannot, and it lets you adjust for imbalances between groups when the comparison is not a clean experiment [@gelman2024]. The first two are what we would be buying here. The third is the one that matters least in this dataset, since `DPI` is set by the experimenter. Harrell goes further and calls a statistical model often the best descriptive tool, even when it is not used for inference [@harrell2015], which is a fair reminder that "describe" and "model" are not opposites. And two more reasons, which this part has not needed but the book will, come from McElreath: when the data are split across many groups with few animals in each, raw group means chase the noise of the small groups, and a model that borrows strength between groups does better [@mcelreath2020]. That is the territory of the multilevel models later in the book.

So the practical rule I would give you is this. If the question is "what happened to these animals", plot them and report means and spreads, and say that this is all you are doing. The moment the question becomes "how much should I expect it to fall in a new cohort, and how sure am I?", you need a model, because only a model carries a claim beyond the sample [@gelman2020]. It is worth saying out loud which side of that line you are on.

## When a line is enough

So when should you reach for a line? Not by running down a checklist. I would rather give you the three things I look at, and let you weigh them.

The first is *what the model is for*. Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari are explicit that which assumptions matter depends on what you do with the model [@gelman2020]: a slope is robust to mild unequal variance, a prediction for one new animal is not, and a causal reading needs conditions that no line supplies. A line is a good *description* when it is a fair summary of the data in hand. It is a good *prediction machine* when its mean is right across the range you will predict into and its spread is honest for the groups you care about. It is a good *explanation* only if the design earns that reading. @tbl-reflection_goals puts the three goals next to what each asks of the line.

| If the goal is to... | A line needs... | Look first at... |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| **Describe** the animals you measured | To be a fair summary of them | Group means against the line, and the raw points |
| **Predict** a new animal | A mean that is right across the range and a spread that is honest for each group | Posterior predictive checks of the mean and the SD by group (@sec-mcmc-model-checking) |
| **Explain** what causes what | Everything above, plus a design and a causal story that justify the reading | The experiment itself (randomization, comparison groups) and, later, a causal diagram (@sec-causal-inference-splines) |

: What a line is asked to do depends on the goal. {#tbl-reflection_goals}


The second is *what the design allows*. This is the lesson of `Condition * DPI`: some questions are closed before analysis begins, and a more flexible model cannot reopen them. If your design has no shams after day 0, no choice of family will tell you whether sham and ischemic trajectories differ. Look at the design table before you look at model options.

The third is *how many animals you have per question*. With 7 to 12 animals per day, a model with a free mean and spread for every day estimated its spreads from very little. A line is a form of borrowing strength: it spends one parameter where the free model spends several, and the cost of that thrift is the assumption of straightness. With plenty of animals per condition, the cost of flexibility drops and a richer model becomes easy to afford. With few, a line may be the only model you can afford, and then the honest course is to say that and to check the assumption you are leaning on, as we did.

None of this is a flowchart, because the questions interact: a modest sample may push you toward a line while a prediction goal pushes you away from it. What I would ask of you is the same thing I asked of myself in this part of the book. Say which bet each choice makes, check the ones a picture can check, and tell your reader about the ones that only you can.

## What else is on the table

Everything above was done with tools from this part, because I wanted you to see how far a careful line goes. Now a look at the road ahead, with one rule: I am not going to teach any of it here. The reason to see it now is so that, the next time a model fails in a way you recognize, you know which drawer to open (@fig-reflection-drawers).

![The line is the first drawer. When a model fails in a way you recognize, you now know which other drawer to open.](images/linear-models-reflection_drawers-of-tools.png){#fig-reflection-drawers fig-align="center" width="45%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden chest of six drawers in a workshop. The top drawer is open and holds a single ruler; the five closed drawers below are painted with a row of dots, two overlapping faces, a pie with one slice missing, a wavy line and three linked rings."}

There are two kinds of change, and the rest of the book is organized around them. The first is [model expansion]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: you do not throw the model away, you let it grow where it fails, the way you would add a lens to a microscope instead of replacing it. @gelman2026 prefer exactly this, a final model that bridges between simpler alternatives, to hard choices between them. Everything in this chapter that went wrong can be put in terms of that growth: the Gaussian breaks, and you grow the family; the single $\sigma$ breaks, and you let it vary; the rows are not independent, and you add the structure that says so.

**You can change the noise.** That is the next part. When the outcome is a count, a yes or no, a proportion or a crossing time, the line keeps its job and the family changes. The PDGFR-β+ counts we met in this chapter are the first case, and [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) explains why a Gaussian that predicts negative cells has to give way to a model that respects what a count is. Three more outcome types follow: @sec-logistic-regression for a pass or a fail, @sec-count-regression for counts with an exposure and extra zeros, and @sec-beta-robust-regression for proportions and crossing times.

**You can change the structure.** That is the part after it. The day-3 spread, which no predictor in this part could absorb, is a job for a model that lets $\sigma$ depend on the day, which the book builds in @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression. The bump followed by a plateau that forced us to cut the time axis is a job for a model that bends, taken up with the whole 0 to 30 day course in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries and with splines in @sec-causal-inference-splines. And the day you analyze several sections or several cells per animal, rows stop being independent, and @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts is the first of the models that handle it.

There are also whole families of approaches this book does not cover, such as rank-based tests or flexible prediction algorithms from machine learning. They answer different questions, and an honest answer to the reviewer's "why this model?" is sometimes "because that other one answers a different question."

Two ideas from the books organize what follows. The first is that the model should follow the goal: whether you want to describe, to predict or to estimate a causal effect changes which assumptions matter and which tools you should use to choose, and McElreath warns in particular against using predictive criteria to pick among causal models [@mcelreath2020]. The second is [model expansion]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: start with the simple model, check it, and extend it (more flexible shape, hierarchical structure, extra data) only where the check fails [@gelman2026]. For a quantity that changes over time, such as tissue area across 30 days, the books present a short list of alternatives to the straight line: polynomials, which are discouraged because they misbehave outside the data and let a point at day 30 move the curve at day 21 [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]; splines and Gaussian processes, which bend the curve locally (`s(time)` and `gp(time)` in `brms`); multilevel growth models, with an intercept and a slope for each animal; and mechanistic growth curves, which build biological facts directly into the equation, such as an area that cannot be negative and a recovery that levels off [@mcelreath2020]. If you read only one explanation of these for a non-statistician, make it McElreath's, whose treatment of splines as local bumps that are added together, and of growth curves written from biological constraints, is the most approachable of the four books. The book returns to several of them in the next part.

## So, why a linear model?

Go back to the margin of the second page. "Why a linear model?" A reason I would be happy to sign: *because the question was how much tissue is lost per day inside the first two weeks; because the outcome is a continuous area that a bell curve describes fairly; because one row per animal makes the rows independent; because I checked the shape and the spread with pictures and the line is fair inside days 3 to 14, which I chose after looking and say so; and because where it was not fair, over the whole month and in the day-3 spread, I say that too.* That is longer than "because it is what I know", and it is a better answer to give a reviewer. It also gives them something to argue with, which is what a methods section is for.

If there is one thing I would like you to carry out of this part, it is that the line was never the point. The point was the question: how much, and how sure are we? A line answered it well in one stretch, badly in another, and could not answer it at all in a third. The next part keeps the question and changes what we mean by noise. On to [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro).
